statements.claim: The Pandavas had lost their kingdom at dice and were living in the great forest in affliction; their friends — the Bhojas, the Vrishnis and the Andhakas, the consanguineous relatives of Panchala, Dhrishtaketu the king of Chedi, and the Kaikeya brothers — came to them with hearts fired with anger against the sons of Dhritarashtra.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: 'Hearing that the Pandavas had been banished, the Bhojas, the Vrishnis, and the Andhakas went to those heroes residing in affliction in the great forest... the consanguineous relatives of Panchala, and Dhrishtaketu the king of Chedi, and... the Kaikeyas, their hearts fired with wrath.'

statements.claim: They asked 'What should we do?' and sat in a wide circle around Yudhishthira the just, with Vasudeva at their head.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: 'reproaching the sons of Dhritarashtra, they said, "What should we do?" And those bulls of the Kshatriya race, with Vasudeva at their head, sat themselves down round Yudhishthira the just.'

statements.claim: Saluting the foremost of the Kurus, Krishna mournfully vowed: 'The earth shall drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna, of Dussasana and the wicked Sakuni! Slaying these in battle... we shall install Yudhishthira the just on the throne. The wicked deserve to be slain. Verily, this is eternal morality.'
statements.evidence: MB 3.12 quotes the vow nearly verbatim, including 'The wicked deserve to be slain! Verily, this is eternal morality.'

statements.claim: On account of the wrongs of Pritha's sons, Janardana fell into such a passion that he seemed bent upon consuming all created things, and Arjuna exerted himself to pacify him.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: 'when on account of the wrongs of Pritha's sons, Janardana had thus got into a passion, and seemed bent upon consuming all created things, Arjuna exerted himself to pacify him.'

statements.claim: Arjuna recited Krishna's former-life feats: ten thousand years as a muni on Gandhamadana, eleven thousand years on water alone at Pushkara, a hundred years standing on one leg on the high hills of Vadari living on air, a twelve-year sacrifice on the Saraswati with body like a bundle of veins, and a thousand celestial years on one leg at Prabhasa.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12 Arjuna's speech itemizes each penance with matching figures (ten thousand years on Gandhamadana, eleven thousand at Pushkara, a hundred years on Vadari on one leg living on air, twelve-year Saraswati sacrifice, one thousand celestial years at Prabhasa).

statements.claim: Arjuna recalled the slaying of Naraka and the first horse-sacrifice, the destruction of Daityas and Danavas until Indra was given sovereignty, the three steps by which the child Krishna filled heaven, firmament and earth, and hundreds of sinful Asuras slain in each of a thousand incarnations.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: 'Slaying the Asura Naraka... thou hadst obtained his ear-rings, and performed... the first horse-sacrifice... slaying... Daityas and Danavas... giving the lord of Sachi... the sovereignty of the universe... fill by three steps only the heaven, the firmament, and the earth... in thy incarnations on those thousand occasions, thou hadst slain... sinful Asuras by hundreds.'

statements.claim: Arjuna said: 'All asceticism rests in thee... thou art the cause of creation and its course... Thou art mine and I am thine, and all that is mine is thine also. O thou irrepressible one, thou art Nara and I am Narayana.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt and passage: Arjuna's speech ends 'Thou art mine and I am thine, while all that is mine is thine also!... O thou irrepressible one, thou art Nara and I am Narayana or Hari!' (the pack's index summary loosely phrases this as Krishna answering; the passage, treated as authoritative, has Arjuna speaking).

statements.claim: Krishna's wrath cooled; he did not unsay the vow that the earth would drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna and that Yudhishthira would be crowned, and the onlookers marvelled at Arjuna, who had calmed him simply by telling Krishna who he was.
statements.evidence: Canonical summary states Arjuna recites the feats 'to calm him'; the cooling of the wrath and the awe of the assembly is connective resolution not literally recorded in the excerpted passage, and it does not contradict the pack.

statements.claim: Krishna's anger frightened his own kinsmen (opening line).
statements.evidence: Dramatic atmosphere consistent with the passage's 'seemed bent upon consuming all created things'; the pack does not record the kinsmen's fear (they are shown arriving in wrath against the Kauravas), so no specific source.

notes: Dialogue and penance catalogue track MB 3.12 (Ganguli) closely; all figures verified against the passage. Two connective-narration items (kinsmen frightened, post-speech calm) are atmosphere/resolution, neither unsupported fact nor contradiction. The pack's index summary attributes the Nara/Narayana line to Krishna, but the passage (authoritative) puts it in Arjuna's speech, as the story does.

statements.claim: In the Kamyaka forest, while the visiting kinsmen talked of vengeance, the weeping Draupadi sat apart, grieving her husbands' loss of everything at dice and their exile.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Vasudeva then spake unto the weeping Draupadi'; MB 3.12 opening (shared passage) shows the kinsmen arriving with wrath over the Pandavas' banishment and affliction in the forest (dice-calamity context established by the arc and by DKS_0378's 'distress begot of dice').

statements.claim: The visitors were the Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas, the relatives of Panchala, the king of Chedi, and the Kaikeya brothers, who sat in a wide circle around Yudhishthira while Krishna at their head vowed the earth would drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna, Dussasana and the wicked Sakuni.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12 passage (reproduced in this pack) lists the visitors verbatim and records Krishna's vow.

statements.claim: Krishna told the weeping Draupadi: 'O fair lady, the wives of those with whom thou art angry shall weep even like thee, beholding their husbands dead on the ground, weltering in blood.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt quotes the sentence verbatim.

statements.claim: Krishna promised: 'I promise thou shalt once more be the queen of kings! The heavens might fall, or the Himavat might split, the earth might be rent, or the waters of the ocean might dry up, but my words shall never prove futile.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt quotes the promise verbatim (continuing '...my words shall never prove futile', matching the pack index summary 'his words never futile').

statements.claim: Draupadi was the princess of Panchala and the shared wife of the five brothers, and the men she was angry with (Duryodhana, Karna, Dussasana, Sakuni) sat in Hastinapura.
statements.evidence: Background framing consistent with the corpus (pack index lists her with the Pandavas; the 3.261 pack passage calls her 'the excellent princess Draupadi, devoted to her husbands'); the specific 'shared wife of five brothers' and the enemies' whereabouts are not re-stated in this pack's excerpt.

statements.claim: Krishna consoled her not with patience or philosophy but with a counter-vow staking the order of nature on his word.
statements.evidence: Connective gloss faithfully summarizing the quoted vow; no new factual assertion.

statements.claim: Even Arjuna, standing among the allies, said nothing; that evening the talk of the gathered kings turned from grief to plans of armies and alliances and the war that waited at the end of thirteen years.
statements.evidence: Arjuna is in the pack's character list for this scene, but his silence and the evening's war-talk are connective staging; the thirteen-year exile figure belongs to the corpus-wide dice-game settlement rather than this pack's excerpt.

notes: Both of Krishna's quoted promises match the 3.12 excerpt verbatim. Remaining items are background or evening atmosphere with no unsupported facts or contradictions.

statements.claim: Krishna told Yudhishthira in the Kamyaka forest: 'If I had been present at Dwaraka, this evil would not have befallen thee' — because he had been away from the Anarta country (Dwaraka's region), engaged against Salwa.
statements.evidence: MB 3.13: 'O lord of earth, if I had been present at Dwaraka... this evil would not have befallen thee!' and 'it is owing to my absence from the Anartta country at that time that thou hast fallen into such distress begot of dice'; pack index summary states the absence was 'while fighting Salwa.'

statements.claim: Krishna said that coming to the gambling match even uninvited by the son of Amvika, Duryodhana, or the other Kauravas, he would have prevented the game by showing its evils, summoning Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and Vahlika to his aid.
statements.evidence: MB 3.13 passage quotes this nearly verbatim ('coming unto the gambling-match, even if uninvited by the son of Amvika (Dhritarashtra), or Duryodhana... summoning to my aid Bhishma and Drona and Kripa, and Vahlika').

statements.claim: He would have told Dhritarashtra his sons should have nothing to do with dice, shown how the son of Virasena was formerly deprived of his kingdom by the evils of dice, and described how a man once engaged in the game keeps playing from desire of victory until ruin, losing possessions, falling into distress, losing untasted wealth, and exchanging harsh words in a single day.
statements.evidence: MB 3.13: 'let thy sons have nothing to do with dice! I would have shown the many evils (of dice) through which... the son of Virasena was formerly deprived of his kingdom... how a man once engaged in the game continueth to play (from desire of victory)... through dice men in a day lose their possessions, and fall into distress, and are deprived of their untasted wealth, and exchange harsh words!'

statements.claim: Krishna named women, dice, hunting and drinking as the four evils that deprive a man of prosperity, with evils attending on all of them per those versed in the Shastras.
statements.evidence: MB 3.13 quotes the four evils and the Shastra opinion verbatim.

statements.claim: Had Dhritarashtra accepted the counsel the welfare of the Kurus and virtue would have been secured; had he rejected it, Krishna would have compelled him by force; and had the false friends at his court supported him, Krishna would have slain them all along with the gamblers in the hall.
statements.evidence: MB 3.13 states each condition and consequence in sequence ('the welfare of the Kurus as also virtue itself would both have been secured... I would have compelled him by force... I would have slain them all, along with those gamblers, there present!').

statements.claim: Krishna said: 'O Kauravya... it is owing to my absence from the Anarta country at that time that thou hast fallen into such distress begot of dice.'
statements.evidence: MB 3.13 quotes the sentence verbatim.

statements.claim: On arriving at Dwaraka Krishna learned of the calamity from Yuyudhana and, his heart sore with grief, came speedily, saying 'Alas! O bull of the Bharata race, ye have all fallen into dire distress. I see thee with thy brothers plunged in misfortune.'
statements.evidence: MB 3.13: 'on arriving at Dwarka I learnt from Yuyudhana all about thy calamity!... with a heart sore agitated by grief, have I speedily come here... Alas! O bull of the Bharata race, ye have all fallen into dire distress! I see thee with thy brothers plunged in misfortune!'

statements.claim: The dice game at Hastinapura (loaded dice, staking and losing wealth, brothers, himself and the queen) led to the Pandavas' thirteen-year exile — the shared story everyone in the circle knew.
statements.evidence: Recap of the prior corpus arc (the dice-game events immediately preceding this episode) that this pack presupposes ('this evil...begot of dice'); the loaded-dice and thirteen-year details are not re-established in the 3.13 excerpt itself but match the corpus canon.

statements.claim: The lament was also a promise in disguise that Krishna would not be absent from whatever game came next; he had been 'fighting his own war at Saubha' when the dice fell.
statements.evidence: Salwa/Saubha is supported by the pack index summary ('absence while fighting Salwa') and MB 3.12's reference to destroying Salwa and the city of Saubha; the closing 'promise in disguise' is narrative reflection.

notes: Krishna's long speech in MB 3.13 is reproduced with high fidelity; all conditional claims (counsel/force/slaying the courtiers) match the passage. Only connective items are the dice-game recap and closing reflection.

statements.claim: Durvasa, having first ascertained that the Pandavas were seated at ease and that Draupadi had finished her meal and was reposing, came to the forest surrounded by ten thousand disciples.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261: 'One day, having previously ascertained that the Pandavas were all seated at their ease and that Krishna (Draupadi) was reposing herself after her meal, the sage Durvasa, surrounded by ten thousand disciples repaired to that forest.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira received the guest with joined palms, pointed to an excellent seat, gave a fit and respectful welcome, and said 'Return quick, O adorable sir, after performing thy diurnal ablutions and observances'; the muni then went with his disciples to the stream to bathe.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 describes the welcome and quotes Yudhishthira's words verbatim ('that sinless Muni, not knowing how the king would be able to provide a feast... proceeded with the latter to perform his ablutions').

statements.claim: The sun-given vessel remained full until Draupadi finished her meal and empty after; she had already eaten, so there was no food for the guests, and she was in great anxiety.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261: Draupadi 'was in great anxiety about the food'; 'The sun-given vessel remains full till I finish my meal. But as I have already taken my meal today, there is no food in it now.'

statements.claim: Draupadi prayed inwardly to Krishna, the slayer of Kamsa, addressing him as son of Devaki, soul/creator/destroyer of the universe, saviour of the afflicted, kind to those who take refuge in him, dark as the blue lotus, red-eyed as the lily, in yellow robes with the Kaustubha gem, and said 'As thou didst protect me before from Dussasana, do thou extricate me now from this difficulty.'
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 quotes the prayer with all these epithets and the closing plea verbatim ('she inwardly prayed to Krishna, the slayer of Kansa').

statements.claim: The great and sovereign God, lord of the earth, of mysterious movements, ever kind to his dependents, perceiving her difficulty, instantly repaired to that place, leaving the bed of Rukmini, who was sleeping by his side.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt quotes this nearly verbatim, including 'instantly repaired to that place leaving the bed of Rukmini who was sleeping by his side.'

statements.claim: Draupadi bowed to him in great joy and told him everything — the arrival of the munis and the empty vessel; Krishna asked for food ('I am very much afflicted with hunger... give me some food without delay'), and when she explained the vessel was empty, insisted it was no time for jest and had her fetch and show him the vessel.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 follows this sequence with the quoted exchanges ('This is no time for jest, O Krishna. I am much distressed with hunger, go thou quickly to fetch the vessel and show it to me').

statements.claim: In the vessel Krishna saw a particle of rice and vegetable sticking at its rim, swallowed it, and said 'May it please the god Hari, the soul of the Universe, and may that god who partaketh at sacrifices be satiated with this.'
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 quotes the finding and the words verbatim.

statements.claim: Krishna told Bhimasena to invite the munis to dinner; Bhima went quickly to the nearest stream of transparent, cool water, where Durvasa and his disciples — having plunged in and rubbed their bodies — found their stomachs full to the throat.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261: 'the long-armed Krishna... said unto Bhimasena, "Do thou speedily invite the Munis to dinner"... Bhimasena quickly went... to the nearest stream of transparent and cool water... observing that they all felt their stomachs to be full... full to the throat.'

statements.claim: The ascetics came out staring at one another, saying the repast had been uselessly prepared since they could not eat, and Durvasa answered: 'By spoiling the repast, we have done a great wrong to that royal sage, king Yudhishthira.'
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 quotes both speeches verbatim.

notes: Very high fidelity: nearly every quoted line matches MB 3.261 (Ganguli) verbatim, including the correct disambiguation of the two 'Krishnas' (the princess Draupadi and the god). Minor glosses (Rukmini 'slept on unaware', atmosphere of Draupadi's despair) are connective only.

statements.claim: Durvasa's ten thousand disciples came out of the stream full — their stomachs heavy to the throat — unable to touch the promised feast.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 (passage reproduced in this pack): the ascetics 'observing that they all felt their stomachs to be full... our stomachs seem to be full to the throat.'

statements.claim: Durvasa understood that they had done a great wrong to the royal sage Yudhishthira by spoiling the repast, and the company fled, fearing the king's wrath, without farewell.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 has Durvasa say 'By spoiling the repast, we have done a great wrong to that royal sage, king Yudhishthira'; the pack's index summary confirms the outcome: 'the frightened Munis flee.' (The passage itself is truncated at this point in the pack, so the flight is per the pack summary.)

statements.claim: The Pandavas' sun-given vessel was empty because Draupadi had already eaten, so no feast could be made; Draupadi prayed to Krishna in Dwaraka, reminding him how he had protected her from Dussasana, and he left Rukmini's bed and came instantly.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 (full passage in this pack) covers the empty vessel, the prayer ('As thou didst protect me before from Dussasana, do thou extricate me now from this difficulty'), and Krishna's instant arrival leaving Rukmini's bed.

statements.claim: Krishna found a single grain of rice and a leaf of vegetable clinging to the vessel's rim, ate it, and in that same hour the sages bathing in the stream felt their hunger die.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261: Krishna 'saw a particle of rice and vegetable sticking at its rim. And swallowing it...' while the ascetics 'having plunged into the river... felt their stomachs to be full.'

statements.claim: Krishna told the Pandavas he had been implored by Draupadi to come and so had come speedily; they need not fear Durvasa, who was gone; and 'Virtuous men never suffer.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt quotes Krishna's words verbatim: 'Knowing, ye sons of Pritha, your danger from that wrathful Rishi, I was implored by Draupadi to come, and (therefore) have I come here speedily. But now ye have not the least fear from the Rishi Durvasa... Virtuous men never suffer.'

statements.claim: Krishna asked the Pandavas' permission to return home, and they gave it freely and watched him go.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt ends Krishna's speech with 'I now ask your permission to let me return home'; pack index summary records that he 'returns home.'

statements.claim: The brothers found it strange comfort given their lives of suffering — the poisoned feast, the lost kingdom, the exile, their wife dragged before the assembly of enemies — yet believed him.
statements.evidence: Connective reflection listing prior corpus events (poisoning by the sons of Dhritarashtra is confirmed in the DKS_0383 pack passage 'gara-dana'; the dice/exile and Dussasana episode are established corpus events).

statements.claim: Yudhishthira, left alone, understood that the protection they had prayed for had been with them all along.
statements.evidence: Closing devotional reflection; no factual assertion requiring source.

notes: Krishna's reassurance speech matches the pack excerpt verbatim. The munis' flight is supported by the pack's index summary (the passage is truncated mid-sentence in the pack file, so the summary is authoritative for that beat). Recap items match the shared 3.261 passage.

statements.claim: Krishna went to Akrura's house accompanied by Balarama (Rama) and Uddhava.
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.11: 'akrūra-bhavanaṃ kṛṣṇaḥ saha-rāmoddhavaḥ prabhuḥ' — Krishna went to Akrura's house together with Rama and Uddhava.

statements.claim: Akrura saw them from afar, bowed to Krishna and Balarama, and was greeted back by them; he held the water of their foot-washing on his head and, having worshipped them, rubbed their feet resting on his lap.
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.12-15: 'nanāma kṛṣṇaṃ rāmaṃ ca sa tair apy abhivāditaḥ / pādāvanejanīr āpo dhārayan śirasā... pādāv aṅka-gatau mṛjan.'

statements.claim: Akrura said: 'By fortune, the wicked Kamsa is slain with all his followers, and this family is yours' and 'Blessed are our dwellings, that the teacher of the world has entered them.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.16: 'diṣṭyā pāpo hataḥ kaṃsaḥ sānugo vām idaṃ kulam'; SB 10.48.24: 'adya... no vasatayaḥ... sa tvaṃ jagad-gurur adhokṣaja... praviṣṭaḥ.'

statements.claim: Akrura praised the two as foremost persons, cause and substance of the world; Krishna creates, sustains and dissolves the universe by his own powers; when the ancient Vedic path is lost he proclaims it for the world's good; and he has now descended into Vasudeva's house by his own portion to lighten the earth's burden, spreading glory over his family.
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.17, 20, 22-23: 'yuvāṃ pradhāna-puruṣau jagad-dhetū jagan-mayau... sṛjasy atho lumpasi pāsi viśvaṃ... sva-śaktibhiḥ... yadā yadā veda-pathaḥ purāṇaḥ... tvayodito 'yaṃ jagato hitāya... vasudeva-gṛhe 'vatīrṇaḥ svāṃśena bhāram apanetum ihāsi bhūmeḥ... kulasya yaśo vitanvan.'

statements.claim: Akrura said Krishna's way is hard to reach even for the kings of the gods, asked what wise man would seek refuge anywhere but in him (dear to devotees, true in speech, a grateful friend who grants every wish), and begged him to cut the bonds of son, wife, wealth, house and body.
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.25-26: 'kaḥ paṇḍitas tvad-aparaṃ śaraṇaṃ samīyād bhakta-priyād ṛta-giraḥ suhṛdaḥ kṛta-jñāt... sarvān dadāti suhṛdo bhajato 'bhikāmān... yogeśvarair api durāpa-gatiḥ sureśaiḥ... chindhy āśu naḥ suta-kalatrā-dhanāpta-geha-dehādi-moha-raśanāṃ.'

statements.claim: Krishna answered that great souls like Akrura are the ones to be served, the most worthy; holy places are not made of water, nor are the gods made of clay and stone — the true sacred presence lives in people, in a well-wishing friend and a heart bowed to the good.
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.29-31 (śrī-bhagavān uvāca): 'bhavad-vidhā mahā-bhāgā niṣevyā arha-sattamāḥ / na hy am-mayāni tīrthāni na devā mṛc-chilā-mayāḥ / sa bhavān suhṛdāṃ vai naḥ śreyān śreyaś-cikīrṣayā.' The last clause is the story's connective gloss of verse 31.

statements.claim: Krishna told Akrura that after Pandu's death his children were left with their mother in great sorrow, and the blind king of Hastinapura (son of Ambika), guided by his wicked son, dealt meanly with his brother's sons; the boys had been brought to the capital after their father's death, not by choice.
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.32-33: 'pitary uparate bālāḥ saha mātrā su-duḥkhitāḥ / teṣu rājāmbikā-putro bhrātṛ-putreṣu dīna-dhīḥ'; pack's rendered excerpt confirms 'the blind king follows his wicked son' and that the Pandavas were 'brought there with their mother after their father's death.'

statements.claim: Krishna commanded: 'Go to Hastinapura and learn how the Pandavas fare — whether things go well with them or ill'; having so commanded Akrura, he (with Rama and Uddhava) departed.
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.34-35: 'gaccha jānīhi tad-vṛttam adhunā sādhv asādhu vā / ity akrūraṃ samādiśya bhagavān harir īśvaraḥ.'

statements.claim: Akrura was the man who had once carried Kamsa's message and come back carrying Krishna's grace instead; he asked for no guard or retinue — a friend's eyes were his only credential.
statements.evidence: Backstory callback to the earlier corpus arc (Akrura's summons of Krishna to Mathura for Kamsa) plus connective staging of his departure; the pack presupposes Akrura's established devotion.

notes: All episode content verifies verse-by-verse against SB 10.48.11-35 (Sanskrit, GRETIL) and the pack's rendered excerpt. Krishna's 'holy places are not made of water, nor gods of clay and stone' speech is correctly attributed to Krishna per the pack's śrī-bhagavān uvāca tag.

statements.claim: In Hastinapura, Kunti — widow of Pandu and mother of five sons the court had never wanted — lived watched on every side in the palace of the Kurus, until word came that her brother Akrura had arrived from Mathura.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49 context: Akrura was sent to Hastinapura (Gajasahvaya) by Krishna per SB 10.48.33-34 (previous pack); SB 10.49.6: 'pṛthā tu bhrātaraṃ prāptam akrūram' — Pritha (Kunti) approached her brother Akrura. Her widowhood/motherhood is the presupposed situation of the episode.

statements.claim: Akrura greeted the elders — Bahlika with his son, Bharadvaja, Gautama — as courtesy required, and then stayed for months, watching, to learn the king's conduct.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.1-3: 'saha-putraṃ ca bāhlīkaṃ bhāradvājaṃ sa-gautamam / yathāvad upasaṅgamya... uvāsa katicin māsān rājño vṛtta-vivitsayā.'

statements.claim: He marked the sons of Pandu's brilliance, energy, strength, courage, humility and other good qualities, and also what the sons of Dhritarashtra had done to them — the giving of poison and other unseemly deeds.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.4-5: 'teja ojo balaṃ vīryaṃ praśrayādīṃś ca sad-guṇān / kṛtaṃ ca dhārtarāṣṭrair yad gara-dānādy apeśalam.' (The 'poison mixed into food' wording is a slight elaboration of gara-dāna.)

statements.claim: Kunti came to Akrura weeping; among her rivals she was like a doe among wolves, and she asked whether her parents and brothers still remembered her.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.6-9: 'api smaranti naḥ saumya pitarau bhrātaraś ca me / ... sapatna-madhye śocantīṃ vṛkānāṃ hariṇīm iva'; pack excerpt: 'Weeping, Kunti said...'

statements.claim: Kunti said: 'The blessed Krishna, my brother's son, is the refuge, dear to his devotees. Krishna, Krishna, great yogin, soul of the universe, protector of all beings! I see no refuge for us but your lotus feet... Salutation to Krishna, the pure one, the supreme self.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.8-12: 'bhrātreyo bhagavān kṛṣṇaḥ śaraṇyo bhakta-vatsalaḥ / ... kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa mahā-yogin viśvātman viśva-bhāvana / nānyat tava padāmbhojāt paśyāmi śaraṇaṃ nṛṇām / namaḥ kṛṣṇāya śuddhāya brahmaṇe paramātmane.'

statements.claim: Akrura and Vidura stood with her, sharing her joy and sorrow; Vidura was the wise uncle of the Kurus who had always loved the Pandavas.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.14: 'sama-duḥkha-sukho 'krūro viduraś ca mahā-yaśāḥ'; Vidura's identity as the Kurus' wise, Pandava-loving uncle is corpus-canonical background.

statements.claim: Having spoken her grief aloud and been heard, Kunti's prayer reached its destination — answered in a friend's promise to carry her words back to Mathura; that night, perhaps, she slept more peacefully.
statements.evidence: Hedged, inward-looking closing ('perhaps... something in her knew'); consistent with Akrura's later report to Krishna in SB 10.49.30 (next story) but not a sourceable event in this pack.

notes: Prayer and lament verified verse-by-verse against SB 10.49.1-14 (Sanskrit, GRETIL). The doe-among-wolves image is the pack's own (vṛkāṇāṃ hariṇīm iva). Only the closing is speculative inner state, clearly hedged.

statements.claim: Before leaving Hastinapura, Akrura — who had come to learn how the Pandavas fared and had learned of the poison and cruelties — asked to see the blind king Dhritarashtra, who sat on the throne his brother had left and loved his own sons with a crooked love.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.15: 'yāsyan rājānam abhyetya viṣamaṃ putra-lālasam' — as he was departing he approached the king who was intensely attached to his sons; Dhritarashtra's blindness and regency are presupposed (SB 10.48.33 'rājāmbikā-putro...').

statements.claim: Akrura counselled: 'Rule the earth by righteousness, and win your subjects by good conduct. Act otherwise, and you will be blamed in every mouth and walk into darkness.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.17-18: 'dharmeṇa pālayann urvīṃ prajāḥ śīlena rañjayan / anyathā tv ācaraṃl loke garhito yāsyase tamaḥ.'

statements.claim: He told the king no one dwells forever with anyone; a being is born alone and dies alone — no retinue follows a man out of the world, and guards cannot surround a grave.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.19-20: 'neha cātyanta-saṃvāsaḥ kasyacit kenacit saha / ekaḥ prasūyate jantur eka eva pralīyate.' The retinue/guards lines are rhetorical elaboration of 'born alone, dies alone.'

statements.claim: Wealth gathered by wrong means is carried off by others of little wit; the man who nourishes his sons on unrighteousness, thinking himself clever, takes the guilt onto his own shoulders and is finally abandoned by those very sons.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.21-23: 'adharmopacitaṃ vittaṃ haranty anye 'lpa-medhasaḥ / puṣṇāti yān adharmeṇa sva-buddhyā tam apaṇḍitam / svayaṃ kilbiṣam ādāya tais tyakto nārtha-kovidaḥ.'

statements.claim: Akrura concluded: 'Therefore this world, O king, is a dream, a waking illusion, a fantasy of the mind. Do not anchor your soul to it.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.24: 'tasmāl lokam imaṃ rājan svapna-māyā-manoratham.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra admitted: 'Even so, gentle one, your sweet words do not rest in my heart, because my heart is unsteady,' and asked 'What man can undo the ordinance of the Lord?' — the lord who, entering his own creation through his inscrutable power, sets in motion the wheel of the world.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.26-28: 'tathāpi sūnṛtā saumya hṛdi na sthīyate cale / īśvarasya vidhiṃ ko nu vidhunoty anyathā pumān / yo durvimarśa-pathayā nija-māyayedaṃ sṛṣṭvā guṇān vibhajate tad-anupraviṣṭaḥ... saṃsāra-cakra-gataye parameśvarāya.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra bowed to that unknowable power and fell silent; the counsel had been given but found no room in his heart.
statements.evidence: Verse 28's salutation ('tasmai namaḥ...') supports the bowing; the 'fell silent' and the closing verdict on the counsel are connective narration consistent with his confessed inability to act.

statements.claim: Back in Mathura, Akrura went straight to Krishna and Balarama and reported everything — the Pandavas' state, what the sons of Dhritarashtra had done, and the blind king's confession — without softening a word.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.30: 'śaśaṃsa rāma-kṛṣṇābhyāṃ dhṛtarāṣṭra-viceṣṭitam' — he reported Dhritarashtra's conduct to Rama and Krishna; the fuller content (Pandavas' treatment and the king's reply) follows from his mission (10.48.34) and the pack summary 'reported all.'

statements.claim: The news did not surprise Krishna and Balarama; from that day a message had passed between Hastinapura and Mathura, and the road between them ran both ways.
statements.evidence: Closing connective imagery; no unsupported factual assertion.

notes: Counsel and reply verify verse-by-verse against SB 10.49.15-30 (Sanskrit, GRETIL); Dhritarashtra's fatalistic reply is faithfully rendered. Elaborative lines (retinue/guards, falling silent) are rhetorical extensions of sourced verses.
